text: This course provides a broad overview of modern methods and tools for big data analytics. Numerical and graphical methods of descriptive statistics are introduced. Data analytic methods are demonstrated using the statistical computing software R.

Numeric vectors are the backbone of data science.

Making numbers out of strings

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Turning strings into numbers
Numbers often arrive as text, typically when data is imported. readr has two parsers for this:

parse_double() for strings that are clean numbers
parse_number() for strings that have extra text around the number

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
parse_number()
parse_number() ignores text before and after the number. That makes it handy for currency, percentages, and similar messy values.













Grouping marks too


Notice that the comma in $1,234 is handled. The result is the number 1234.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Counting with count()
Much of data science is counting and adding. dplyr’s count() gives a quick tally of how many rows have each value.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The long way
count() is a shortcut. Building it by hand lets you compute extra summaries in the same step.













n() only works inside dplyr verbs


n() takes no arguments and returns the size of the current group. Outside of summarize(), mutate(), or filter(), there is no “current group”, so it fails.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Useful count variants: n_distinct()
n_distinct(x) counts the unique values of x. Which destinations are served by the most carriers?

text:
Weighted counts
A weighted count is a sum. For example, the total distance each plane has flown:

text:
Counting missing values
Combine sum() with is.na() (recall TRUE counts as 1). How many flights per destination were cancelled, meaning dep_time is missing?

What is a transformation?
Transformation functions return a vector the same length as the input: a natural fit for mutate().
This section covers:

Arithmetic and recycling rules
Minimum and maximum
Modular arithmetic
Logarithms
Rounding
Cutting numbers into ranges
Cumulative and rolling aggregates

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Arithmetic and recycling rules
You can use +, -, *, /, and ^ on vectors. When the two vectors have different lengths, R recycles the shorter one by repeating it until it matches the longer one.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Recycling when the lengths don’t divide evenly
text:
Recycling when the lengths don’t divide evenly
Recycling a longer vector works silently if the lengths divide evenly, and gives a warning if they don’t.













Tidyverse is stricter


Base R is permissive about recycling. The tidyverse is stricter and generally only recycles single values.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: A silent recycling bug in filter()
text:
A silent recycling bug in filter()
Recycling also works with comparisons, which can quietly give wrong answers:













No error, wrong answer


This compares month with 1, 2, 1, 2, ... row by row. It does not ask “is month 1 or 2?”. It only keeps January flights in odd-numbered rows and February flights in even-numbered rows.
The fix is %in%, which you met last lecture.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Minimum and maximum: pmin() and pmax()
text:
Minimum and maximum: pmin() and pmax()
Two kinds of min and max exist:

pmin() and pmax() work row by row across vectors (the “p” is for parallel)
min() and max() summarize everything into one value

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The summary versions
Compare with min() and max(), which collapse all the values:













Key idea


Every row gets the same answer from min() and max(): the smallest and largest value in both columns combined. Use pmin() and pmax() for a per-row answer.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Modular arithmetic
Modular arithmetic is division with a quotient and a remainder:

%/% is integer division (how many whole times it fits)
%% is the remainder

sched_dep_time stores a time as a number like 1530, meaning 15:30. We can split it into hour and minute:

Cancellations by hour of the day
Using the hour trick, we can see how the proportion of cancelled flights changes through the day.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Logarithms
Logarithms turn multiplicative relationships into additive ones, and they help with data that spans many orders of magnitude. R has three:

log(): natural log (base e)
log2(): base 2
log10(): base 10

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Which log should I use?







Recommendation



Use log2(): it’s easy to interpret. Each +1 on the log scale means the original value doubled; each -1 means it halved.
Use log10(): when you want to back-transform easily, since each +1 means ×10.





The inverse of a log is exponentiation:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Rounding
round(x) rounds to the nearest integer. The digits argument controls where to round, and it can be negative.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
floor() and ceiling()

floor() always rounds down
ceiling() always rounds up
Neither has a digits argument, so you scale first

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Cutting numbers into ranges
cut() chops a numeric vector into bins and returns a factor. You supply the break points, and they don’t need to be evenly spaced.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Custom labels
Give labels one fewer element than breaks, because there is one fewer bin than break points:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Values outside the breaks
Anything outside the breaks becomes NA:













Open-ended bins


Use -Inf and Inf as the outer breaks so nothing falls off the ends. Bins are right-closed by default, like (5, 10]; pass right = FALSE to make them left-closed, like [5, 10).

















More helpers


ggplot2 also offers cut_interval(), cut_number(), and cut_width() for common binning patterns. They live there mainly because histograms need them.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Cumulative and rolling aggregates
Cumulative functions keep a running total (or running min, max, mean) as they move down the vector:

cumsum(), cumprod(), cummin(), cummax() in base R
cummean() from dplyr

Prerequisites

This part uses stringr, part of the tidyverse
We also use the babynames package for example data (names of babies born in the US over many years)








Finding stringr functions


Every stringr function starts with str_. In RStudio, type str_ and the autocomplete list shows all of them, with a documentation panel for whichever one is highlighted.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Quotes
You create a string with either single or double quotes. There is no difference in behaviour between them.













Style


The tidyverse style guide recommends double quotes, unless the string itself contains double quotes.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Forgot to close the quote?
If you forget the closing quote, R shows the continuation prompt + and waits for more input:
> "This is a string without a closing quote
+
+
+ HELP I'M STUCK IN A STRING







Getting unstuck


Press Escape (esc) to cancel the unfinished input and get your prompt back.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Escapes
To put a quote character inside a string that uses the same quote, you escape it with a backslash. Because the backslash is itself special, you escape a literal backslash with another backslash.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Printing vs. viewing







The printed string is not the string


When R prints a string, it shows the escapes (the backslashes). To see the raw contents, use str_view().











x shows "\\" for the backslash, but str_view(x) shows a single \
Base R’s writeLines() also shows the raw string








Display in the browser


str_view() normally uses color to show spaces, tabs, and matches. In the browser console, that styling may look different or be missing, but the raw characters are still shown.

text:
Exercise







Live exercise


Create strings that contain each of these values:

He said "That's amazing!"
\a\b\c\d
A run of backslashes, for example \\\\\\

x2 <- "\\a\\b\\c\\d"
x3 <- "\\\\\\\\\\\\"

str_view(c(x1, x2, x3))

text:
Combining fixed text with data
So far we’ve made one string at a time. A common job is to combine fixed text with values from your data. Three functions work well inside mutate() and summarize():

str_c()
str_glue()
str_flatten()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
str_c()
str_c() takes any number of vectors and returns a character vector. It’s similar to base R’s paste0(), but it follows tidyverse recycling rules and handles missing values consistently.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
str_c() in mutate()













Missing values are contagious


Just like in arithmetic, if any input is NA, the result is NA. The fourth greeting is missing.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
str_glue()
str_c() gets awkward with many pieces. str_glue() (from the glue package) lets you write the whole string in one go, with { } marking code to evaluate.













NA behaves differently


Unlike str_c(), str_glue() converts a missing value to the text "NA".

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Literal braces in str_glue()
To include an actual brace, double it:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
str_flatten()
str_c() and str_glue() return one result per input. str_flatten() goes the other way: it collapses a vector into a single string. That makes it a summary function, so it fits in summarize().







The second argument is the separator
last sets a different separator just before the final item (for an “Oxford comma” style list)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
str_flatten() by group













Base R


The base R equivalent is paste() with the collapse argument.

Diagnosing widening problems
separate_wider_delim() expects every string to split into the same number of pieces. Real data often doesn’t.

Too few pieces in some rows

The function errors rather than guessing, and the message tells you what to try

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Too few: debug mode
too_few = "debug" keeps the result but adds diagnostic columns, named after the input column:

x_ok: did this row split cleanly?
x_pieces: how many pieces it had
x_remainder: any leftover text

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics

Too few: fixing it
Once you understand the problem, tell the function what to do. "align_start" fills the missing pieces with NA at the end; "align_end" fills them at the start.

Too many pieces
The same idea works in the other direction, using too_many:













Here x_remainder holds the extra text

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Too many: fixing it
Two choices for the extra pieces:

too_many = "drop" discards them
too_many = "merge" glues them onto the last column














Same principles elsewhere


separate_wider_position() and separate_wider_regex() have the same too_few and too_many ideas.

Length: str_length()
str_length() counts the characters in each string. A missing value gives NA.

text:
Aesthetics at a glance



Aesthetic
Controls
Mapping example




x, y
position
aes(x = displ, y = hwy)


color
outline / point color
aes(color = class)


fill
interior color (bars, areas)
aes(fill = class)


shape
point symbol (≤6 levels)
aes(shape = drv)


size
point/line size (continuous only)
aes(size = cty)


alpha
transparency (continuous only)
aes(alpha = year)









Important


Inside aes() = mapping, which is driven by data and you get a legend.
Outside aes()= setting, which is essentially a fixed constant, no legend.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mapping vs. setting







Mapping


Ties an aesthetic to a variable in your data. The value changes per row, and ggplot2 draws a legend. Written inside aes().











Setting


Gives an aesthetic one fixed value for every point, no matter what the data says. No legend, since there’s nothing to decode. Written outside aes().




# Mapping: color depends on class, varies per point, gets a legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class))

# Setting: every point is blue, no legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")







Trap


geom_point(aes(color = "blue")) looks like a setting but is written inside aes(), so it’s a mapping to the constant string "blue", producing one default-palette color and a stray one-entry legend.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stats and after_stat()
Every geom has a default stat that computes what actually gets plotted. For geom_bar(), that default is count: the number of rows in each group. You never have to ask for it explicitly.







after_stat()


Lets you reach into the stat’s output and ask for a different computed variable instead of the default:



Variable
Definition




count
number of observations per group (default)


prop
proportion of the total each group represents


density
count standardized so the area under the curve sums to 1








ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) + geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Count vs. proportion vs. density
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "count (default)")
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "prop")
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500) +
  labs(title = "density")



















Note


Same data, same bars, three different y-axes. count shows raw group sizes; prop rescales so every bar’s height reflects its share of the whole (summing to 1 across bars); density is more commonly used with histograms/freqpolys and re-scales for area rather than height, here it looks nearly identical to prop since geom_bar() bins are all width 1.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The EDA loop
EDA is not a procedure with a checklist. It’s a cycle you run until the questions stop being interesting:

Generate questions about your data
Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modelling
Refine your questions, or generate new ones from what you found

Most of what you produce during EDA gets thrown away, and that’s okay!

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Why it’s not optional







Important note


Dead ends are expected and not failure.




Even when the research question arrives fully formed, you still have to know whether the data can answer it.







Data cleaning


A special case of EDA: you’re asking whether the data meets your expectations, and using the same tools like visualization, transformation, modelling to find out.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two Guiding Questions

What variation occurs within my variables?
What covariation occurs between my variables?








Variation


How much a single variable’s values differ from one observation to the next. Even measuring the same quantity repeatedly gives slightly different results, and real differences between subjects or across time add even more spread.











Covariation


The tendency for two or more variables to move together. If two variables covary, knowing the value of one improves your guess about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A simple example
Weigh 10 apples from the same tree:
142g, 138g, 151g, 145g, 149g, 133g, 156g, 144g, 140g, 147g
That spread, some apples heavier, some lighter, is variation: natural differences within one variable, even from apples off the same tree.
Now also measure each apple’s diameter:



Diameter (cm)
Weight (g)




6.5
133


7.0
140


7.8
151


8.1
156



Bigger diameter tends to mean more weight. The two variables move together, that’s covariation. Knowing one lets you make a real guess about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation







Variation


The tendency of a variable’s values to change from one measurement to thenext.





Even a perfectly constant quantity will read slightly differently each time you measure it. That’s measurement noise.
Real variables also differ between subjects and over time on top of that noise, and the combination gives every variable its own characteristic shape.
Some cluster tightly, some spread wide, some have several common values.
You can’t see that shape in a long column of numbers. Plotting the distribution is how you see it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The Diamond Data







The diamonds variables





Variable
Meaning




price
price in US dollars


carat
weight of the diamond


cut
quality of the cut: Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal


color
diamond color, from J (worst) to D (best)


clarity
how clear the diamond is: I1 (worst) to IF (best)


x, y, z
length, width, depth in mm


depth
total depth percentage


table
width of the top of the diamond relative to widest point

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A first look

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Changing the Binwidth

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)


Same data. A much narrower bin reveals structure the first plot hid entirely.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Typical values: what to ask







Checkpoint



Which values are most common? Why?
Which are rare? Does that match what you expected?
What are the gaps?
Are there unexpected patterns? What could explain them?





For the carat histogram: why the spikes at whole carats and common fractions? And why more diamonds just above each spike than just below?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Clusters mean subgroups
When a distribution separates into clumps, you can ask yourself:

How are observations within a cluster alike?
How do clusters differ from each other?
What explains the split?
Could the clusters be an artifact rather than real structure?

::: {.callout-important title”Recall from last week”} The three clusters from Financial Wellness data: stressed, coping, and comfortable. :::

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Unusual values hide in plain sight
text:
Unusual values hide in plain sight

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)


The only hint of anything odd is how wide the x-axis is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zoom in on the y-axis

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zooming In
Now three unusual regions show up: near 0, around 30, and around 60.







coord_cartesian()


The bars are still computed from all the data, so you can safely zoom the y-axis to see rare bins without changing what got counted.
ylim()/xlim() instead discard any data outside the limits before the stat runs, which can silently change your bar heights.
When you just want a closer look, reach for coord_cartesian().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Outliers
A value that sits far away from the rest of a variable’s values, unusual enough that it stands out from the general pattern. Outliers can come from a few different places:







A real, unusual observation


The value is correct. It just represents something genuinely rare, an extremely large diamond, an exceptionally tall person.











A measurement or data entry error


The value is wrong. A typo, a broken sensor, a missing value coded as 0 instead of NA. This is common and worth checking first.











Why they matter


An outlier can quietly distort summaries like the mean or a fitted trend line, so it’s worth investigating rather than ignoring. But it should never be dropped automatically just because it’s inconvenient, understanding why it’s unusual comes first.




You can’t always spot an outlier from a column of numbers. Plotting the distribution, and sometimes zooming in, is usually what reveals it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Pull the outliers out

unusual <- diamonds |>
  filter(y < 3 | y > 20) |>
  select(price, x, y, z) |>
  arrange(y)

unusual

# A tibble: 9 × 4
  price     x     y     z
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  5139  0      0    0   
2  6381  0      0    0   
3 12800  0      0    0   
4 15686  0      0    0   
5 18034  0      0    0   
6  2130  0      0    0   
7  2130  0      0    0   
8  2075  5.15  31.8  5.12
9 12210  8.09  58.9  8.06

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What we found
y is a dimension in millimeters. A diamond cannot be 0 mm wide, so those are missing data encoded as zero.

You wouldn’t have been able to find these simply by searching for NA as missing data.

The 32 mm and 59 mm entries are implausible too!






Important


This is the core payoff of EDA: visualizing the data surfaced a data-quality problem that a search for NA never would have. Always sanity-check units and physically-plausible ranges, not just missingness flags.









Caution


Run your analysis with and without the outliers. If it barely moves and you can’t explain them, dropping them is defensible. If it moves a lot, find the cause and disclose the removal in your write-up — don’t drop values without justification just because they’re inconvenient.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two ways to handle them

# Option 1: drop the whole row — usually too blunt
diamonds2 <- diamonds |> filter(between(y, 3, 20))

# Option 2: replace the bad value with NA — usually better
diamonds2 <- diamonds |>
  mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))







Note


filter() basically isolates the rows where the y values are between 3 and 20, while keeping the rest of the variables (as long as their corresponding y is between 3 and 20). It discards the rest.
mutate() changes (like mutation) the column of y such that if y is less than 3 OR y is greater than 20, then the corresponding y value becomes NA.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values in plots
ggplot2 won’t guess where to put an NA, so it drops them and warns you. Silence the warning with na.rm = TRUE (only once you’ve understood why they’re missing).

diamonds2 <- diamonds |> mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Explore the distributions of x, y, and z in diamonds. Which is length, which width, which depth?
Explore price. Try a wide range of binwidths. Anything surprising?
How many diamonds are 0.99 carat vs. exactly 1 carat? Why the gap?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Covariation
If variation describes behavior within a variable, covariation describes behavior between variables: the tendency for two or more variables to move together.
The strategy depends on the variable types:

categorical × numerical
categorical × categorical
numerical × numerical

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Categorical × numerical:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)









The Count Problem


Group sizes differ so much that shape differences are invisible. Do you think each cut share the same pattern?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Switch the y-axis to density
Density is the count standardized so the area under each curve is 1. Since it isn’t a column in the data, after_stat() fetches it from the stat. The following plot is a frequency polygon.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Frequency polygons vs Boxplots
Fair diamonds (the lowest quality cut) appear to have the highest average price.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reordering
cut is an ordered factor, so its order is meaningful. Most categorical variables aren’t.







Ordered Cuts


It goes from Fair -> Good -> Very Good -> Premium -> Ideal.











What do you do if the categories are: Apples, Oranges, Bananas?


This fct_reorder(variable, by, fun) function sorts factor levels by a summary statistic (e.g. mean/median) of another variable, which almost always makes a categorical-vs-numeric plot easier to read at a glance.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Example
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Flip when labels are long
Swap the x and y mappings with no extra function needed:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median))) +
  geom_boxplot()

text:
Your turn






Try it yourself


Recall that there are variables such as price, carat, cut, color, clarity, x, y, z, depth, and table.
Earlier we saw that Fair cut diamonds look more expensive on average than Ideal cut diamonds, which may be the opposite of what you’d expect. carat (the diamond’s weight) turns out to be the strongest predictor of price in the whole dataset.

Plot price against carat. Does the relationship look strong?
Now plot carat against cut. Is carat spread evenly across cut qualities, or do Fair diamonds skew toward one end?
Why does Fair diamonds skewing that way in carat make them look pricier overall, even though a worse cut should, on its own, lower the price?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Categorical × categorical: counts

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = color)) +
  geom_count()


Circle area shows how many observations fall at each combination.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Numerical × numerical

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point()


Would you argue that there is a lot of overplotting in this figure?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Transparency helps

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1 / 100)


Clusters at 1, 1.5, and 2 carats become visible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Bin + Boxplots ?

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(group = cut_width(carat, 0.1)))


cut_width(x, width) slices x into equal-width bins. Can you comment on this plot?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Interrogating a pattern
A systematic relationship shows up as a pattern. When you spot one, try and ask yourself:

Could this be coincidence?
How would you describe the relationship?
How strong is it?
What other variables might be involved?
Does it hold within subgroups?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation vs. covariation
Variation is uncertainty within a single variable. If price varies a lot on its own, knowing nothing else, you can’t say much about what a given diamond costs. Covariation between variables cuts that uncertainty down.






Tip


If carat and price covary, then knowing a diamond’s carat narrows down your guess for its price a lot more than guessing blind. The stronger the covariation, the more one variable tells you about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Modelling
This is the entire logic behind prediction and modelling: a useful predictor is just a variable that covaries with the outcome you care about. A variable that doesn’t covary with the outcome is useless as a predictor, no matter how interesting it looks on its own.

E.g. income with financial wellness








Correlation does not imply causation?


Covariation is not the same as causation. Two variables can covary because one causes the other, because both are driven by a third variable, or by pure coincidence.

E.g. The divorce rate in Maine correlates with per capita margarine consumption

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

EDA is a loop:

ask questions
→ visualize/transform/model
→ formualte better questions

Variation within a variable: typical values, clusters, unusual values
Outliers are sometimes errors, sometimes discoveries. Investigate before deciding; disclose what you removed.
Covariation between variables: pick the technique by variable type

Next: turning exploratory graphics into ones other people can read.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Recap: Day 1 of Whole Game

We examined some EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis): with variables like income, benefits, delayed paycheque difficulty, etc.
We ended with three financial wellness clusters: Stressed, Coping, Comfortable
Today: we look at how we actually got there , … including the messy parts of data analytics …

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Before we look at the raw data…
text:
Before we look at the raw data…







Thinking Moment


What do you think could go wrong with real, raw survey data?











Potential Problems


What kinds of problems might it have that yesterday’s polished plots didn’t show?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Here’s the actual raw file

survey_2017_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2017.csv")

# Note the skip = 1 -- 2022's file has a stray metadata line above the
# real header (a leftover from the export on the new survey platform)
survey_2022_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2022.csv", skip = 1)

glimpse(survey_2017_raw)
glimpse(survey_2022_raw)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Duplicate responses (rows)
A few respondents show up more than once. - Think of this as a double-submitted survey.

survey_2017_raw |> count(respondent_id, sort = TRUE) |> filter(n > 1)

survey_2017_raw <- survey_2017_raw |> distinct()
survey_2022_raw <- survey_2022_raw |> distinct()


The function distinct() removes exact duplicate rows. It is always worth checking for before doing anything else), since duplicates quietly inflate every count.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Tidy data: benefits are stuck in wide format

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions







The format for income response is a mess!


Sometimes people are allowed to type in their responses however they like. For example, if someone has an annual income of $85,000, there are several ways they might enter that in the survey:

"85000"
"$85,000"
"85,000"
"85K"

So how do we take all these different formats and turn them into something we can actually work with in our analysis?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Recall from last week’s survey
For Question 7 of the survey, I asked everyone what was the best sandwich?







Most Popular Answer


Grilled Cheese was among the most popular answers. But this is what I got from last week’s survey response:

Grilled cheese
Grilled Cheese
Grilled Cheese!
grilled cheese
grilled cheese with Hot sauce
Grilled cheese sandwich
Ham Grilled Cheese

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: provinces
Same province, several spellings: "Ontario", "ON", "ontario ".

standardize_province <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("ontario", "on") ~ "Ontario",
    x %in% c("alberta", "ab") ~ "Alberta",
    x %in% c("british columbia", "bc") ~ "British Columbia",
    x %in% c("quebec", "qc") ~ "Quebec",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(x)
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: Yes/No
We might get three variations for the same two answers: "Yes"/"No", "Y"/"N", "yes"/"no".

standardize_yn <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("yes", "y") ~ "Yes",
    x %in% c("no", "n") ~ "No",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing data







Where did missing data come from?


Sometimes we don’t always get all the complete data set that we want.

People tend to skip questions that they don’t feel comfortable answer.
perhaps people forgot to fill in one of the questions/pages of survey.
maybe people gave some weird looking answer that is unusable (e.g $*@2#$1aE&)
or sometimes these questions are simply irrelevant to them

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 1) Delete the row
If a respondent didn’t answer a question in the survey, we can just remove this person entirely from the data analysis. :)







This is cool, but…


While this is a simple method, you will lose the respondents.

if the people who skipped the question aren’t random, the ones left behind don’t represent everyone fairly.






survey_2017_nomiss <- survey_2017_clean |>
  drop_na(income, savings_pct,
          debt_overwhelmed,
          emergency_fund_likelihood)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 2) Imputation
Instead of throwing the whole response away, we can guess a reasonable value to put in its place.

like using the average of everyone else’s answer. (e.g. mean or median)


survey_2017_clean |> mutate(income = ifelse(is.na(income), median(income, na.rm = TRUE), income))








This is cool, but…


Now some of your “data” is really just a guess. If you fill in too many values this way, your data can look more similar than it actually is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched response







Too many response levels


Sometimes survey designers choose a set of response options one year, then decide to change them the next. For example, in our financial wellness data, the survey asked questions of How difficult is it to obtain $2,000 of emergency fund?:

in 2017, there are 7 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Somewhat difficult, Neither, Somewhat manageable, Manageable, Very manageable
in 2022, there are now only 5 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Neither, Manageable, Very manageable

So what do you do? Neither of them directly match each other. And this is difficult for a year-to-year comparative analysis

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Potential Solution







Compromise


We can collapse both down to 3 levels — Difficult, Neither, Manageable.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult", "Somewhat difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Somewhat manageable", "Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Before: 7 Levels vs 5 Levels

Different number of categories, different wording. It is not easy to tell how people have changed over time by comparing these two bar plots side by side as-is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
After:

Now that both years use the same 3 levels, we can finally put them side by side and ask: did things get better, worse, or stay the same?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Different ways of asking the same question
text:
Different ways of asking the same question







Mismatched question: same question, different name


Sometimes a question gets worded differently across years, even though it’s really asking the same thing.

in 2017, the survey asked How difficult was it for you if your paycheque is delayed?

stored as paycheque_delay_difficulty

in 2022, the question became If there is a two week delay in your paycheque arrival, how impactful would it be to your finances?

stored as twoweek_pay_delay_impact


Same underlying question, different wording and different column name — rename() fixes this in one line each.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched responses: Age

survey_2017_clean |> select(age) |> head()
survey_2022_clean |> select(age) |> head()








Are you willing to share your age?


Sometimes the same underlying question gets measured differently across years, even when the intent is identical.

in 2017, respondents gave an exact age

stored as age, e.g. 34

in 2022, respondents picked from age brackets instead

stored as age, e.g. "30-40"

Now we have the same underlying question, but a different level of precision

In order to compare over the years, everyone needs to speak the same bucket language.







survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(age_bucket = case_when(
    age <= 30 ~ "18-30",
    age <= 40 ~ "30-40",
    age <= 50 ~ "40-50",
    age <= 65 ~ "50-65",
    TRUE ~ "65+"
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  rename(age_bucket = age)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Removed benefit option: aligning categories







Non-existent Option in Survey


“Educational funding” existed as a choice in 2017, but the 2022 platform dropped it. To compare years fairly, we fold anything not offered in both years into a shared “Other” category.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(benefit_preference = if_else(
    benefit_preference == "benefit_education",
    "benefit_other",
    benefit_preference
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Combine into one data set

survey_combined <- bind_rows(survey_2017_clean, survey_2022_clean)

glimpse(survey_combined)








Only possible now


Now that we have:
— column names match (rename()) - category sets match (the “Other” recoded) - response scales match (the 3-level of likert responses in paycheque question)
Every fix so far existed to make this one line possible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Too much info in one column
text:
Too much info in one column







One column doing two jobs


The variable respondent_id looks like a single value, but it’s actually smuggling in two separate pieces of information at once.

the year the response came from, e.g. 2017
the respondent’s number within that year, e.g. 0001

Both are jammed into one string: "2017-0001". If we ever want to work with just the year, or just the respondent number, we’re stuck first pulling them apart.





survey_combined <- survey_combined |>
  separate(respondent_id, into = c("survey_year", "respondent_num"), sep = "-")

survey_combined |>
  select(survey_year, respondent_num, everything()) |>
  head()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Show concluding results

survey_combined |>
  ggplot(aes(x = financial_wellness_cluster, y = income, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  labs(title = "Income by Cluster: 2017 vs 2022",
       x = "Cluster", y = "Income ($)", fill = "Year") +
  theme_minimal()


This is the exact plot style from Day 1, except now you’ve watched every step of how the data underneath it got here.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Back to your predictions







Discussion


Which of your guesses from the start of class came true?
What did we run into that nobody predicted?











Document your decisions


A results plot without its cleaning log is a claim without evidence. For any real report, this deserves its own short section (ahem your final report):

Which rows/columns were dropped, and why
Every recoding decision (e.g. collapsing levels and combining buckets, etc.)
What’s imputed vs. observed, clearly marked

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A few cautions







Keep in mind



Every cleaning choice was also an analytical choice — a different 3-level collapse, a different age-bucket rule, a different imputation method could all shift what we find downstream
This dataset is synthetic: today’s numbers are illustrative, not a claim about real Canadians
Later this semester: missing-data methods and statistical tests that let you make these calls more rigorously than by eyeballing












Next Week


We will actually begin learning how to code! Starting with Visualization.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Missing values come in three kinds
text:
Missing values come in three kinds
We’ve met NA before (in plot warnings, summaries, and the logical vectors lecture). Now we go deeper:

Explicit missing values: an NA you can see
Implicit missing values: a row that isn’t there at all
Empty groups: a category with no observations (usually from factors)








Where the tools live


Most of the tools here come from dplyr and tidyr.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What to expect
Explicit missings are NAs in the data. This section covers tools for creating and removing them:

Last observation carried forward: fill()
Fixed values: coalesce() and na_if()
NaN

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Last observation carried forward
Some data entry (often by hand) uses a blank to mean “same as the row above”. This is called last observation carried forward.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
fill()
fill() replaces each NA with the most recent non-missing value above it:















Look at what got filled


everything() filled every column, including response. Here that would wrongly copy a response value into a missing one. Fill only the columns where a blank really means “same as above”:



















Unusual patterns


fill() has a .direction argument for other cases, such as filling upward ("up") or both ways.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Fixed values: coalesce()
Sometimes a missing value stands for a known fixed value, usually zero. coalesce() replaces NAs with a value you choose:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Fixed values: na_if()
The reverse problem: older software uses a sentinel value like 99 or -999 to mean “missing”. na_if() turns it into a real NA:















Sentinel values corrupt your statistics


If -99 stays in the data, it is treated as a real number: mean(c(1, 4, 5, 7, -99)) is dragged far below reality.



















Fix it at import time


If you know about the sentinel when reading the file, declare it up front with the na argument: read_csv(path, na = "99"). Use na_if() when you discover the problem later.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
NaN
NaN (“not a number”) is a close cousin of NA. It appears from impossible math:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
NaN behaves like NA















is.na() catches both


is.na() returns TRUE for both NA and NaN. Usually you don’t need to tell them apart. If you do, use is.nan():

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What is missing?







Explicit vs. implicit



An explicit missing value is the presence of an absence
An implicit missing value is the absence of a presence





Explicit missings are NAs you can see. Implicit missings are rows that were never recorded.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Example data: stocks

stocks <- tibble(
  year  = c(2020, 2020, 2020, 2020, 2021, 2021, 2021),
  qtr   = c(   1,    2,    3,    4,    2,    3,    4),
  price = c(1.88, 0.59, 0.35,   NA, 0.92, 0.17, 2.66)
)


The price for 2020 Q4 is explicitly missing (NA)
The price for 2021 Q1 is implicitly missing: there is no row at all








Implicit missings hide from summaries


mean(price, na.rm = TRUE) and count() silently skip rows that don’t exist. You won’t get a warning, so you have to go looking for them.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Making implicit “missing” explicit
pivot_wider() needs a cell for every combination, so the gaps become visible NAs:









Now both missing values are explicit NAs

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Pivoting back
pivot_longer() keeps those NAs by default. If they are only there because of the table’s shape (structurally missing), drop them with values_drop_na = TRUE:















Think before dropping


values_drop_na = TRUE also drops the real explicit NA (2020 Q4). Only use it when every NA is just a gap in the table’s shape.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
complete()
complete() generates every combination of the variables you name, adding explicit NA rows where they were missing:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
complete() with a known range
complete() only knows the values that appear. If the full range is bigger, supply it:















full_seq()


full_seq(x, 1) generates every value from min(x) to max(x) in steps of 1, which is handy for filling in a range of years or days.



















When complete() isn’t enough


Build the full set of rows by hand, then combine it with dplyr::full_join(). You’ll meet joins later in these slides.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values found by joins
Some missing observations only show up when you compare one table to another. anti_join(x, y) keeps the rows of x with no match in y.
Destination airports in flights that are missing from the airports table:








Plane tail numbers in flights that are missing from planes:









Four airports and hundreds of planes have no record: implicit missing data

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Empty groups
A final kind of missing is an empty group: a category that exists but has no observations. This is most common with factors.
Here every person is a non-smoker, but the factor knows about both levels:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Counting drops empty groups















The ‘yes’ group vanished


By default, count() shows only the levels that occur. Anyone reading this table wouldn’t know “yes” was even possible.




Keep empty groups with .drop = FALSE:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The same issue in ggplot2
ggplot2 also drops unused levels of a discrete variable:








Force them to show with drop = FALSE:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Empty groups in summarize()
With .drop = FALSE in group_by(), the empty group stays, and the summary functions run on a zero-length vector:

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reading the empty-group row
For the “yes” group (no data):

n = 0: correct, there are no rows
mean_age = NaN: the mean of nothing is 0 / 0
min_age = Inf and max_age = -Inf: the minimum of nothing is “infinitely large”
sd_age = NA








Inf and -Inf are not data


These values are not wrong, but they are not meaningful ages either. They come from summary functions running on a vector of length 0, which is different from NA (length 1).











Why Inf?


It makes combining results work: min(c(x, y)) is always equal to min(min(x), min(y)), even when x is empty.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A simpler alternative: complete()
Summarize first, then add the missing group with complete():















The count is now NA instead of 0


The upside is explicit NAs instead of NaN and Inf. The downside is that n also becomes NA, when the true count is 0. Choose the approach that fits your question.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing Data summary

Explicit missings: fill(), coalesce(), na_if(), and NaN
Implicit missings: pivot, complete(), and joins (anti_join())
Empty groups: .drop = FALSE and complete()








The habit to keep


Before analysing, ask: what could be missing here, and in what form? An NA, a missing row, or an empty group each need different tools.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics

The idea in one picture
Two lists, and neither one answers the question alone:















A join glues two tables together using something they share


Here the shared column is animal. It’s called the key.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Joining the lists









Mia and Sam get a sound
Leo’s unicorn isn’t in the sound list, so his sound is NA: a missing value

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text: What if something doesn’t match?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Types of Joins







Two families of joins



Mutating joins (left_join(), inner_join(), …) add columns from another table
Filtering joins (semi_join(), anti_join()) keep or drop rows based on a match












Why joins matter


Real questions almost always need several tables (flights, airlines, weather, planes). Joins combine them, and unmatched rows are where missing data and bugs sneak in.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Primary and foreign keys

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table
A foreign key is a column that matches the primary key of another table









Table
Primary key
Matched by in flights




airlines
carrier
carrier


airports
faa
origin, dest


planes
tailnum
tailnum


weather
origin and time_hour (a compound key)
origin and time_hour










Same name, different meaning


year in flights is the departure year. year in planes is the year the plane was built. Don’t assume a shared name means a shared key.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Check that a key is really a key
text:
Check that a key is really a key
Count by the key and look for rows where n > 1. An empty result means no duplicates:















Also check for missing keys


A key with an NA can’t identify anything: planes |> filter(is.na(tailnum))











Unique today is not the same as a valid key


In airports, alt and lat happen to be unique for all rows but one pair. A key should be something that should identify a row, not something that happens to be unique. If there’s no good key, add a surrogate key with mutate(id = row_number()).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
left_join(): add columns
left_join(x, y) keeps every row of x and adds columns from y.















A left join keeps all of x


The result should have the same number of rows as x. If it doesn’t, investigate.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
When there’s no match
No match in y? The row of x stays, and the new columns are NA:















Unmatched rows become NA, silently


left_join() never warns you. Check afterward with anti_join() or sum(is.na(...)).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The natural join trap
By default, left_join() matches on every column the two tables share:















Almost everything is NA!


It matched on tailnum and year, but the two years mean different things, so almost nothing matched.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Fix it with join_by()
Say which key you mean:









The two year columns are kept apart as year.x and year.y

When the key columns have different names, name both sides:















Always specify the key


Even when a natural join happens to work, join_by() protects you if a column is later added to either table.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
semi_join() and anti_join()
Filtering joins don’t add columns and never duplicate rows.

semi_join(x, y) keeps rows of x that have a match in y
anti_join(x, y) keeps rows of x that have no match in y
















Check every join


Before trusting a left_join(), run anti_join() on the same keys. It shows exactly which rows will get NAs.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The four mutating joins











Join
Keeps rows from
Unmatched rows get NA in




inner_join()
only matches
none (they’re dropped)


left_join()
all of x
y columns


right_join()
all of y
x columns


full_join()
all of x and y
both










Inner joins drop rows silently


Don’t use inner_join() for a plain “add columns” task unless you want to lose unmatched rows. Prefer left_join() and check for NAs.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Matching more than one row

No match: row dropped (inner) or filled with NA (outer)
One match: row kept as-is
Multiple matches: row duplicated, once per match
















Many-to-many: usually a mistake


Key 2 appears twice in both tables, so every x row matches every y row and rows multiply. dplyr warns you. It often means a “key” isn’t unique. If you really want it, add relationship = "many-to-many".











Compare row counts after every join


An unexpected change in nrow() is the earliest sign that a key isn’t what you thought.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Beyond ==
So far every join matched equal keys (equi joins). Non-equi joins match on other conditions.







Type
What it does




Cross join
every row of x with every row of y


Inequality join
matches with <, <=, >, >=


Rolling join
inequality join keeping only the closest match


Overlap join
matches ranges that overlap or contain a value


















Row counts multiply


A cross join of n rows with m rows gives n × m rows. Easy to blow up on big tables.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Rolling join: the closest match
Give each employee the most recent party on or before their birthday:















Edge cases fall through


Ava was born before the first party, so she gets NA. Use anti_join() to find rows like her.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Overlap join: ranges
between(x, lower, upper) matches a value inside a range:















unmatched = “error”


Makes the join fail loudly if any employee has no party, instead of silently dropping them.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Joins summary

Keys: primary keys identify rows, foreign keys point to other tables
Mutating joins add columns: left_join(), inner_join(), right_join(), full_join()
Filtering joins keep or drop rows: semi_join(), anti_join()
Non-equi joins: cross, inequality, rolling, overlap








Join checklist



Name the key explicitly with join_by()
Check the key is unique where you expect it to be
Compare row counts before and after
Run anti_join() to see what didn’t match

Data Science
A concept that is still in the making, may take many shapes and forms for different people. Key ideas:

Look at data from the point of view of a scientist: do experiments, make hypothesis, test hypothesis by more experiments, rinse and repeat, …, arrive at some conclusion.
Look at decision making of all kinds from the point of view of data: tell / refute a story with data, make / break a decision by data, persuade / disillusion using data…

Data Science
Data science is a tool. The correctness of the conclusion not only depends on the correctness of the inputs, but also depends on interpretation. It is also important that the tool is used responsibly.

The science: math, statistics, computer programming, etc.
The output: figures, diagrams, reports, presentation, etc.
The hope: try to be useful, and hopefully helpful. (to whom?)

R is a programming language for statistical computing and graphics

R is software is open source unlike some other statistical software.

R Console

Can give R direct instructions via the R console.

A text file containing a set of commands and comments.
Can create an R script, with the file extension ‘.R’.

Base R

Contains some basic functions and visualization tools.
The base R functions contain only a tiny fraction of what is actually available.

R packages

A package is essentially a suite of related functions that were created by one or more R users.
Currently over 19000 R packages available at https://cran.r-project.org/.

The main packages we will use:

tidyverse.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics

Initializing R packages

Use install.packages("package_name") in the console to install R packages on your own machine.

Example: install.packages("ggplot2") to install ggplot2.

Use library(package_name) to initialize already installed packages.

Example: library(ggplot2) to load ggplot2.

To install the package if it isn’t already installed and then initialize it after installation:

if(!require(package_name)) install.packages("package_name")
library(package_name)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Assigning Variables

The operators =, <-, and -> can be used to assign values to variables

If we want to assign x = 2; x=2, x<-2, and 2->x are equivalent.
Common convention is to use <- but feel free to use =.

Rules for variable names.

Start with a letter (x5 is OK but 5x is NOT.)
Consist of letters, numbers, underscores, and periods (x_5 and x.5 are OK but not x-5).
Case sensitive (x and X would be different variables).

Variable naming conventions

Try to use meaningful names.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Displaying Output

R will display the outputs of unassigned calculations

exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) (approximately) and display the result.

R suppresses the output of assigned calculations

x<-exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) and store the result in x but would not display anything.
To see that value of x we would need to run print(x) or just x.

Workspace (Environment)

Use ls() or objects() to generate a list of objects. in workspace.
Use rm() to remove objects from the current workspace.

The call rm(x,y,z) will remove the variables x, y, and z from the workspace.
The call rm(list=ls()) will remove all objects from the workspace.
The workspace is automatically cleared when RStudio is exited.

What’s the take-away message from the plot above (labelled Figure 2)?

 The blue team always wins. If you score 4 goals, you're guaranteed to win. Scoring more goals than the other team only has a slight correlation with winning the game. Taking more shots has a very slight correlation with scoring more goals.

Figure 2 used veritcal jittering for the number of goals. Why?

 for display purposes. The jittering is done because goals is a continuous variable but was only measured to the nearest whole number; jittering makes it continuous rather than discrete. This jittering is inapproriate - it implies that there were games with 4.2 goals which is impossible. Since goals are whole numbers, all games with, say, 20 shots and 4 goals will be plotted in the exact same spot. Jittering allows us to see this.

From the plot above (Figure 2), how many shots do you need to take in order to have more than a 50% chance to win the game?

 20 40 60 It is impossible to tell from this plot.


In Figure 2, does it appear that shooting more makes you more likely to win?


Answer

Not really! As you take more shots you get more goals, but perhaps your opponent shoots more as well. If you look at, say, 20 shots in a game, it looks like slightly more than half of the games were won. If you look at 40 shots, it still looks like slightly more than half of the games were won.
It really matters what the opponent does!



What is the interpretation of the plot above (Figure 3)?

 The number of shots is uncorrelated with whether the team wins - it's still a 50-50 chance. There's more variation at the extremes because there were fewer games with that number of shots. The overall chance of winning is not exactly 50% because very few of the values are actually 50%. This plot shows how many games a team won at each number of shots. If a team takes 60 shots, they are guaranteed to lose, but if they take exactly 55 shots they have a 75% chance of winning. During a game, a team should stop shooting when they hit 55 shots.

A survey asks respondents for their country, and answers come back as “Canada”, “canada”, and “CAN”. Why do we need to clean these entries before creating a summary chart?

 It changes the numbers from integers to decimals. R will automatically delete all responses that aren't spelled correctly. R will automatically throw an error and refuse to make the plot The computer treats them as 3 completely separate responses.

You want to compare the relative proportions of car classes across different drive types (drv), ensuring that every bar reaches 100% height regardless of the total count in each drive category. Which position adjustment should you use in geom_bar()?

 position = “fill” position = “dodge” position = “stack” position = “identity”

I want to examine the distribution of a single continuous variable (hwy mileage) to check for bimodality and skewness across the entire dataset. Which geometric object is best suited for this task?

 geom_bar() geom_boxplot() geom_histogram() geom_point()

You plot City Mileage (cty) vs. Highway Mileage (hwy) for 234 cars using geom_point(). When you look at the plot, you only see about 100 dots. What is happening, and why is this plot misleading?

 Multiple cars have identical rounded mileage values, causing their points to land on exact same coordinates and stack directly on top of each other. Over half of the cars in the dataset have missing mileage values. geom_point() only plots a random sample of the data when datasets exceed 100 rows. Cars with identical highway and city mileage automatically cancel each other out on the graph.

I created a histogram of continuous highway gas mileage (hwy) using geom_histogram(). By default, ggplot2 uses 30 bins and displays a warning suggesting that the user pick a better binwidth. What happens to the story the plot tells if the student sets an extremely small bin width (e.g., binwidth = 0.1) versus an extremely large bin width (e.g., binwidth = 20)?

 An extremely small bin width converts the plot into a boxplot; an extremely large bin width converts it into a scatterplot. An extremely small bin width only plots outliers; an extremely large bin width only plots the median. ggplot2 automatically rejects bin widths smaller than 1.0 with a fatal error. An extremely small bin width creates too much visual noise (individual spikes), while an extremely large bin width over-smooths the data and hides features like bimodality or skewness.

When we want to deal with outliers, it is better to apply “filter(…)” so that we can isolate (and only work with) data without outliers, rather than using the “mutate(…)” function to change these outlier values to NA instead.

 False True

 They show up as -999 They are not visible at all The NA values are outliers, and tidyverse has automatically removed them from the data set. They show up as zero, 0

 The tendency of two variables to move together The number of bins used in a histogram The tendency of a single variable's values differ from one measurement to the next A coding error that produces incorrect plots

A violin plot shows two distinct humps for one group. What does a boxplot of the same group most likely fail to reveal?

 That the group actually has two common value ranges rather than one smooth distribution  Whether outliers exist The group's median value The exact sample size of the group

 Both are examples of covariation Both are examples of variation Sleep hours night to night = variation; cups of afternoon coffee vs. hours slept = covariation Sleep hours night to night = covariation; cups of afternoon coffee vs. hours slept = variation

A regular expression (regex or regexp) is a concise language for describing patterns in strings.

Escaping
If . means “any character”, how do you match a literal dot? You escape it with a backslash: \.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Choosing How to Show Data







Quick distinctions



Continuous: a numeric value that can (in theory) take any value in a range.
Categorical: falls into one of several unordered groups (nominal) or has only two options (binary).
Likert: an ordered scale (e.g., “very difficult” → “difficult” → … → “very manageable”)

categorical, but with a meaningful order.













One idea to hold onto


The type of variable decides the type of plot.

One category at a time → bar chart
One number at a time → histogram
Two things at once → scatterplot (or boxplot, if one is a category)

Where we are
In this week, I will give you a working template for plots. This chapter explains why that template works.

My Plan

Setup

library(tidyverse)

We’ll work mostly with two datasets that ship with ggplot2:

mpg — 234 car models, 11 variables
diamonds — ~54,000 diamonds


mpg |> select(manufacturer, model, displ, hwy, class, drv) |> head(4)
